query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework, explicitly trained via active learning on ab initio free-energy data (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling contributions), can predict the fusion and high‐temperature thermodynamic free energies of both solid and liquid states with comparable fidelity to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) but at a fraction of its computational cost—even for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental or binary systems at temperatures near melting, with extension to select multicomponent (high-entropy) alloys.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an entropy-aware MLIP where training data consist of targeted ab initio free energy evaluations sampled via active learning. This training focuses on ensuring that vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects are accurately captured, by incorporating free-energy corrections obtained from short, high-accuracy AIMD runs. Then deploy the MLIP in free-energy integration calculations to determine both solid and liquid phase free energies.
generation.conditions: Applied to systems ranging from elemental and binary alloys to moderately complex multicomponent alloys across the temperature window near the melting (fusion) point.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP serves as a computational mediator that reproduces the ab initio potential-energy surface with embedded free-energy corrections and entropy contributions, effectively generating reliable phase free-energy landscapes.
generation.mechanism: By training the MLIP on selective, high-quality ab initio free energy and force data—including corrections for vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-coupling effects—the model learns both the static and thermal fluctuations of the system. Once trained, the MLIP can perform free-energy integration via efficient molecular dynamics, thereby providing accurate phase free energies at a computational cost that is orders of magnitude lower than full AIMD simulations and more efficient than TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: The MLIP should yield phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., melting temperature, entropy changes) with fidelity comparable to that of explicit AIMD free energy evaluations (errors within roughly 5–10%) while reducing computation time by roughly 10– to 100-fold compared to AIMD and offering improved throughput relative to TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics combined with conventional free-energy integration methods and the TOR-TILD method as applied to elemental or binary systems.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to work reliably for systems from pure elements and simple binaries up to moderately complex high-entropy alloys, and within a temperature range spanning near the fusion point (melting temperatures) where vibrational and anharmonic effects remain significant.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of speed-up and error margins may vary with system complexity. Extensions to very complex multicomponent systems might introduce subtle inaccuracies if the training data do not fully capture all relevant entropy contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative binary alloy (e.g., Ni-Al) near its melting temperature and a high-entropy alloy system. For each, perform free-energy integration using (i) the newly developed MLIP approach and (ii) full AIMD free-energy simulations as well as TOR-TILD (for the binary system). Compare the predicted phase free energies and derived properties (e.g., predicted melting temperature and latent heat) from the MLIP with those from the AIMD and TOR-TILD methods.
measurements: Phase free energy differences between solid and liquid states
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP predictions deviate by more than approximately 10% from the AIMD-derived free energies or if the predicted melting temperatures and entropy changes fall outside this error margin, or if the MLIP does not demonstrate a significant reduction in computation time (e.g., less than a 10-fold improvement), then the hypothesis is falsified.
